lessons.title: The news
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Mia check the morning news in the newsroom.

items.example: Mia is reading a new science magazine at her desk.
items.note: Say 'magazine' for a thin book with pictures and stories that comes out every week or month.

image.describe: a colourful glossy magazine lying open on a wooden newsroom desk

items.example: We have breaking news about the big storm near the coast.
items.note: Use 'breaking news' for an important event that is happening right now.

items.example: The photo of the space station is on the front page.
items.note: The 'front page' is the first page of a newspaper where the biggest stories go.

image.describe: the front page of a newspaper showing a picture of a cat astronaut on a desk

items.example: Smarty wrote a report about the new library in town.
items.note: Use 'a report' for a spoken or written description of what happened.

items.example: A good writer always checks a source before sharing news.
items.note: Say 'a source' for the person, book, or website where information comes from.

items.example: I read a headline about an ancient coin discovery this morning.
items.note: Use 'a headline' for the short, big title at the top of a news story.

practice.prompt: Look at the picture on the desk. What is it?
practice.answer: magazine
practice.explanation: A magazine is a thin publication with photos and stories.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose the exact sentence you hear.
practice.audio: There is breaking news about the train station.
practice.answer: There is breaking news about the train station.
options: There is breaking news about the train station.
There is a new book at the train station.
There is a big storm near the train station.
practice.explanation: Breaking news is urgent news arriving right now.

practice.prompt: Match each news phrase with its meaning.

pairs.right: the first page of a newspaper
the name of a news story
where the news comes from

practice.explanation: The headline is the title, the front page is page one, and a source gives the facts.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence about Smarty's work.
practice.text: Smarty is writing ___ about the science experiment.
practice.answer: a report
practice.explanation: You write a report to give full details about an event or experiment.

practice.prompt: Put the words in order to talk about the newspaper.
practice.answer: The big story is on the front page.
practice.explanation: Notice the word order: on the front page.

practice.prompt: Choose the right phrase to finish the sentence.
practice.text: We must check ___ before we print this headline.
practice.answer: a source
practice.explanation: Checking a source makes sure the facts are reliable.

practice.prompt: Read this newsroom line aloud.
practice.text: Look at the headline on the front page!
practice.answer: Look at the headline on the front page!
practice.explanation: Great pronunciation of headline and front page.

practice.prompt: Which sentence sounds natural?
practice.answer: I enjoy reading a music magazine on Sunday.
options: I enjoy reading a music magazine on Sunday.
I enjoy reading a breaking news on Sunday.
I enjoy reading a source on Sunday.
practice.explanation: Use 'enjoy + -ing' with a countable noun like a magazine.

story.hook: What big story is on the front page this morning?

image.describe: Inside a busy newsroom: Smarty the black cat and Mia stand by a large desk covered with newspapers, magazines, and glowing screens.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Good morning, Mia! I just bought this newspaper at the newspaper stand.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Look at that huge headline on the front page!

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Yes! There is breaking news about a new comet near our planet.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Did a journalist write a full report about it?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: She did. Her article is in this morning edition, and she checked a reliable science source.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Amazing! Let us read the science magazine after we finish this page.

questions.prompt: Where did Smarty see the headline?
questions.explanation: Mia says: Look at that huge headline on the front page!

questions.prompt: What is the breaking news about?
questions.explanation: Smarty says there is breaking news about a new comet.

questions.prompt: What do Smarty and Mia want to read later?
questions.explanation: Mia says: Let us read the science magazine after we finish this page.

mission.setup: You are helping Smarty prepare the morning news desk. Answer in your own words.

turns.smarty: Welcome to the newsroom! Do you prefer reading a newspaper or a magazine?
turns.example: I prefer a magazine.
turns.hint: Say whether you prefer a newspaper or a magazine.

turns.smarty: We just got breaking news! Where should we put the big headline?
accept: ^we should put it on the front page$
turns.example: On the front page.
turns.hint: Tell Smarty to put it on the front page.

turns.smarty: Good idea. Should we check a source before we write a report?
accept: ^of course(?: we must check a source)?$
turns.example: Yes, we should check a source.
turns.hint: Agree that checking a source is important.

exposure.gloss: a person who writes news stories
a piece of writing in a newspaper or magazine
one version of a newspaper or magazine
a small street shop that sells newspapers and magazines

lessons.title: TV and radio
lessons.scenario: Sam and Leo watch different shows on the newsroom screen.

items.example: Which channel has the evening news report?
items.note: Use 'channel' for a TV or radio station that shows programmes.

image.describe: a television screen showing a news channel icon with a globe and a cat presenter

items.example: Pass me the remote control so I can change the channel.
items.note: A 'remote control' is the small device you hold to control a TV from across the room.

image.describe: a black television remote control with colourful buttons resting on a sofa

items.example: We are watching a documentary series about life in the ocean.
items.note: Say 'a documentary series' for a set of real-life TV programmes about one topic.

items.example: I always turn on English subtitles when I watch a French film.
items.note: Use 'subtitles' for the words at the bottom of the screen that translate or show speech.

items.example: The news presenter spoke clearly during the morning show.
items.note: Say 'a presenter' for the person who introduces and hosts a TV or radio programme.

items.example: Millions of fans watched the concert on a live broadcast.
items.note: A 'live broadcast' is a TV or radio programme shown at the exact moment it happens.

practice.prompt: Look at the picture. What do you use to change the TV channel?
practice.answer: remote control
practice.explanation: A remote control lets you change channels from your sofa.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose what Sam says.
practice.audio: The subtitles help me understand the show.
practice.answer: The subtitles help me understand the show.
options: The subtitles help me understand the show.
The presenter helps me understand the show.
The remote control helps me change the channel.
practice.explanation: Subtitles show the spoken words on the screen.

practice.prompt: Match the TV and radio words with their descriptions.

pairs.right: the one who speaks on a TV show
a show happening right now on air
many true TV shows about one thing

practice.explanation: A presenter hosts the show, a live broadcast is real-time, and a documentary series has several parts.

practice.prompt: Complete the sentence.
practice.text: The space launch is on ___ five right now.
practice.answer: channel
practice.explanation: TV stations are numbered as channels, like channel five.

practice.prompt: Arrange the words to describe the programme.
practice.answer: We watched a documentary series about big tigers.
practice.explanation: Say 'a documentary series about...' to describe the topic.

practice.prompt: Choose the right phrase for a show happening right now.
practice.text: Do not miss the ___ from the stadium this evening.
practice.answer: live broadcast
practice.explanation: A live broadcast shows an event as it happens.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence aloud.
practice.text: The presenter read breaking news on this channel.
practice.answer: The presenter read breaking news on this channel.
practice.explanation: Clear stress on presenter and breaking news.

story.hook: Why is Leo looking for the remote control in the newsroom?

image.describe: Sam and Leo the cats sitting on a newsroom sofa in front of a large wall screen while Smarty holds a small microphone.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Leo, where is the remote control? The space programme starts soon!

questions.explanation: Sam says: Channel three. It is a live broadcast from the space station.

questions.prompt: Why does Leo ask for subtitles?
questions.explanation: Leo sees that the presenter is speaking Japanese and wants subtitles.

questions.prompt: Where was the remote control?
questions.explanation: Leo says: Here it is, next to the magazine.

mission.setup: You are watching TV with Smarty in the newsroom. Answer in your own words.

turns.smarty: I have the remote control! Do you want to watch a documentary series or a comedy?
turns.example: I want to watch a documentary series.
turns.hint: Tell Smarty which programme you want to watch.

turns.smarty: Good choice! The programme is in Spanish. Shall I turn on the subtitles?
turns.example: Yes, turn on the subtitles.
turns.hint: Ask Smarty to turn on the subtitles.

turns.smarty: Look, the presenter is on air! Is this a live broadcast?
accept: ^no(?: it is not a live broadcast)?$
turns.example: Yes, it is a live broadcast.
turns.hint: Say whether it is a live broadcast.

exposure.gloss: a news forecast about rain, sun, and temperature
a TV game where players answer questions to win prizes
one single part of a TV or radio series
a short pause in a TV show for advertisements

lessons.title: He said that
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Zara share what the presenters said in the newsroom.

items.example: He said that the live broadcast was exciting.
items.note: Use 'He said that' to report what a boy or man said without naming the listener.

items.example: She told me that the report was on her desk.
items.note: Use 'She told me that' when a girl or woman spoke directly to you—always include a person after 'told'.

items.example: They said they were ready for the evening news.
items.note: When reporting 'We are...', change 'we are' to 'they said they were'.

items.example: I thought that the headline was very surprising.
items.note: Say 'I thought that' to share an idea or belief you had in the past.

items.example: In the interview, he explained that the machine was safe.
items.note: Use 'he explained that' when someone gave clear reasons or details.

items.example: The presenter finished the report, and she added that sunny weather was coming.
items.note: Use 'she added that' to report one extra piece of information someone gave at the end.

grammar.title: Reported statements: say and tell
grammar.explanation: When we report what someone said, present verbs usually shift back into the past: am/is becomes was, and are becomes were. Use say without an object (He said that...), and use tell with a person (She told me that...).
examples: He said that the train was delayed.
She told me that they were in the newsroom.

practice.prompt: Choose the right phrase. Notice the word 'me' is not there.
practice.text: ___ the documentary series was on channel two.
practice.answer: He said that
practice.explanation: Use 'He said that' when there is no person object like 'me' or 'him'.

practice.prompt: Mia spoke directly to you. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: ___ the source was reliable.
practice.answer: She told me that
practice.explanation: Use 'told me' when someone speaks directly to you.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose what Zara reports.
practice.audio: They said they were tired after the live broadcast.
practice.answer: They said they were tired after the live broadcast.
options: They said they were tired after the live broadcast.
He said that he was tired after the live broadcast.
She told me that she was tired.
practice.explanation: For a group ('We are tired'), report it as 'They said they were tired'.

practice.prompt: Match each reporting phrase with its best use.

pairs.right: saying why something is true
telling one more thing at the end
sharing your own past idea

practice.explanation: Explained gives reasons, added gives extra information, and I thought shows your past idea.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence reporting what the presenter did.
practice.answer: First he explained that the dog was ready.
practice.explanation: Present 'is ready' shifts to past 'was ready' after 'he explained that'.

practice.prompt: You believed the news was true yesterday. Which phrase starts your sentence?
practice.answer: I thought that
practice.explanation: Use 'I thought that' to talk about what you believed earlier.

practice.prompt: Say this reported sentence aloud.
practice.text: She told me that the headline was on the front page.
practice.answer: She told me that the headline was on the front page.
practice.explanation: Notice how 'is' becomes 'was' in reported speech.

story.hook: What did the scientist say about the strange lights in the sky?

image.describe: Zara and Smarty the cats standing beside a newsroom whiteboard with notes and arrows while watching a presenter on a monitor.

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: Smarty, did you hear the presenter on channel one?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: No! What did he say?

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: He said that bright green lights were over the mountain last night.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: I thought that it was just lightning from a thunderstorm!

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: Well, a space scientist came on, and he explained that it was a comet.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Mia also called me. She told me that they were filming a report now, and she added that the photos were amazing!

questions.prompt: What did Smarty think the lights were at first?
questions.explanation: Smarty says: I thought that it was just lightning from a thunderstorm.

questions.prompt: How did the scientist explain the lights?
questions.answer: He explained that it was a comet
options: He explained that it was a comet
He said that it was snow
He added that it was a cloud
questions.explanation: Zara says: he explained that it was a comet.

questions.prompt: What did Mia tell Smarty?
options: They were going to a shop
questions.explanation: Smarty says: She told me that they were filming a report now.

mission.setup: Smarty missed the morning meeting. Report what your friends said.

turns.smarty: Sam said: 'The report is ready.' How do you report that to me?
accept: ^he said(?: that)? the report was ready$
^sam said(?: that)? the report was ready$
turns.example: He said that the report was ready.
turns.hint: Start with 'He said that' and change 'is' to 'was'.

turns.smarty: And Mia spoke to you earlier: 'The source is reliable.' What did she tell you?
accept: ^she told me(?: that)? the source was reliable$
^mia told me(?: that)? the source was reliable$
turns.example: She told me that the source was reliable.
turns.hint: Start with 'She told me that' and change 'is' to 'was'.

turns.smarty: What about Ben and Leo? They said: 'We are in the newsroom.'
accept: ^they said(?: that)? they were in the newsroom$
turns.example: They said they were in the newsroom.
turns.hint: Use 'They said they were' to report what Ben and Leo said.

exposure.gloss: to announce something publicly and firmly
to speak about something briefly
to reply rudely to someone
to speak very softly so few hear

lessons.title: Review
lessons.scenario: Smarty quizzes you on headlines, TV programmes, and reported statements in the newsroom.

practice.answer: On the front page

practice.prompt: Match the news and TV words with their meanings.

pairs.right: news that comes right now
the writing at the bottom of a screen
the one who speaks on a TV show

practice.explanation: Breaking news is urgent, subtitles appear on screen, and a presenter hosts the programme.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose the sentence you hear.
practice.audio: He explained that the live broadcast was on channel four.

options: He explained that the live broadcast was on channel four.
She added that the magazine was on the table.
They said they were watching a documentary series.

practice.prompt: Complete the reported sentence.
practice.text: Ana spoke to me and ___ the magazine was interesting.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence reporting what the journalists said.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence aloud.

practice.answer: I thought that the documentary series was amazing.

mission.setup: Review what you learned in Lessons 1–3 with Smarty.

turns.smarty: Tell me one thing you can read in the newsroom: a magazine or a remote control?
turns.example: You can read a magazine.

turns.smarty: How do you report this sentence from Mia to you: 'The live broadcast is great.'?
accept: ^she told me(?: that)? the live broadcast was great$
^mia told me(?: that)? the live broadcast was great$

turns.hint: Use 'She told me that' and change 'is' to 'was'.

accept: ^he said(?: that)? he was a presenter$

lessons.title: Reporting verbs
lessons.scenario: Ben and Ana read dramatic headlines from around the town.

items.example: The team vowed to win the championship next year.
items.note: Use 'vow' in headlines and stories when someone makes a serious, strong promise.

items.example: The weather report warned us that a big storm was coming.
items.note: Say 'warn' when someone tells you about danger or a problem before it happens.

items.example: Ana suggested that we check another source for the story.
items.note: Use 'suggest' when someone offers an idea or plan for others to consider.

items.example: Ben admitted that he forgot to save the report.
items.note: Say 'admit' when someone agrees, often unwillingly, that something is true or that they made a mistake.

items.example: The driver denied that he was late for the bus.
items.note: Use 'deny' when someone says that a claim or accusation is not true.

items.example: Smarty insisted that every fact in the article was true.
items.note: Say 'insist' when someone states firmly that something is true or must happen, even when others disagree.

grammar.title: Reporting verbs
grammar.explanation: Instead of repeating say or tell, choose a reporting verb that shows the speaker's attitude: warn (danger), vow (strong promise), suggest (an idea), admit (accept a mistake), deny (say something is not true), or insist (say very firmly).
examples: She warned us that the road was icy.
He admitted that it was his mistake.

practice.prompt: Match each reporting verb with its meaning.

pairs.right: tell someone about a problem
say that something is true
say that something is not true
say that you will do it

practice.explanation: Warn = danger, admit = accept truth, deny = say not true, vow = strong promise.

practice.prompt: The presenter told drivers about heavy snow. Choose the best verb.
practice.text: The presenter ___ drivers that the mountain road was dangerous.
practice.answer: warned
practice.explanation: Use 'warned' when someone tells others about danger.

practice.prompt: Sam said he did not eat the last piece of cake. Choose the best verb.
practice.text: Sam ___ that he ate the chocolate cake.
practice.answer: denied
practice.explanation: Use 'denied' when someone says they did not do something.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose the sentence you hear.
practice.audio: Mia suggested that we watch the live broadcast together.
practice.answer: Mia suggested that we watch the live broadcast together.
options: Mia suggested that we watch the live broadcast together.
Mia insisted that the live broadcast was boring.
Mia admitted that she missed the live broadcast.
practice.explanation: Listen for 'suggested that we watch'.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence showing how strongly Zara spoke.
practice.answer: Zara insisted that her source was reliable.
practice.explanation: Insisted shows that Zara stood firmly behind her source.

practice.prompt: Which headline uses 'vow' correctly?
practice.answer: Scientists vow to help the clean river.
options: Scientists vow to help the clean river.
Scientists vow that the rain was cold.
practice.explanation: Vow means to make a strong promise to do something.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence aloud.
practice.text: He admitted that it was his mistake.
practice.answer: He admitted that it was his mistake.
practice.explanation: Nice clear pronunciation of admitted.

story.hook: Who took Smarty's lucky pen in the newsroom?

image.describe: Ben, Ana, and Smarty the cats gathered around a newsroom desk looking for a missing golden pen.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: My lucky blue pen is gone! Yesterday I warned everyone not to move things on my desk.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: I deny that I lost it! I used my own pencil all morning.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Ben is right. He insisted that he never touched your desk, Smarty.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Hmm, did someone invite a guest into the newsroom earlier?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Wait—I admit that I opened the window, and a little bird flew in!

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Look near the window! I suggest that we check under that magazine—and I vow to help you find it!

questions.prompt: What did Ben deny?
questions.explanation: Ben says: I deny that I lost it!

questions.prompt: What did Ben admit?
questions.explanation: Ben says: I admit that I opened the window.

questions.prompt: Where did Ana suggest checking?
questions.explanation: Ana says: I suggest that we check under that magazine.

mission.setup: Smarty is writing dramatic headlines and needs the right reporting verbs.

turns.smarty: A big storm is coming! Should the headline say 'Scientists warn of storm' or 'Scientists deny of storm'?
turns.example: Scientists warn of storm.
turns.hint: Choose the verb that signals danger.

turns.smarty: Now Leo made a mistake on the front page and said 'Yes, it was me.' Did he admit it or deny it?
accept: ^he admitted that it was his mistake$
turns.example: He admitted it.
turns.hint: Use 'admit' or 'he admitted it'.

turns.smarty: What do you suggest we do to fix the front page?
accept: ^i suggest(?: that)? we check a source$
^i suggest(?: that)? we write a new headline$
turns.example: I suggest that we check a source.
turns.hint: Start with 'I suggest that we...' and give an idea.

exposure.gloss: to say something is true without proof yet
to say that you are unhappy about something
to prove that a report or fact is true
to ask someone to come to an event or place

lessons.title: Social media
lessons.scenario: Lily and Omar check what is popular online in the newsroom.

items.example: That travel influencer has thousands of fans online.
items.note: An 'influencer' is someone popular on social media whose posts and opinions many fans follow.

image.describe: a stylish young cat filming a video on a smartphone with a bright ring light

items.example: Add a hashtag so readers can find all the science posts together.
items.note: Use 'a hashtag' for a word or phrase with # in front of it that groups online posts by topic.

items.example: A funny video of a dancing cat can go viral in one hour.
items.note: Say 'go viral' when a photo, video, or story spreads very quickly across the internet.

items.example: Do not share fake news that has no reliable source.
items.note: Use 'fake news' for false stories made to look like real news online.

items.example: Omar left a friendly comment under Lily's new photo.
items.note: Say 'a comment' for a short message someone writes below an online post or article.

items.example: When you follow someone online, you see their new posts right away.
items.note: Use 'follow someone' when you subscribe to see a person's updates on social media.

practice.prompt: Look at the picture of the cat filming with a ring light. What is this job called?
practice.answer: influencer
practice.explanation: An influencer makes videos and posts for online followers.

practice.prompt: Match the social media phrases with what they mean.

pairs.right: very fast online
a story that is not true, shared as news
a short reply under a post
a name with # on a post

practice.explanation: Viral posts spread fast, fake news is untrue, a comment is a reply, and a hashtag groups topics.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose what happened to the video.
practice.audio: Our science video went viral yesterday evening.
practice.answer: Our science video went viral yesterday evening.
options: Our science video went viral yesterday evening.
Our science video was fake news.
No one left a comment on our video.
practice.explanation: Went viral is the past form of go viral.

practice.prompt: Complete the warning about online stories.
practice.text: Always check the source so you do not share ___.
practice.answer: fake news
practice.explanation: Fake news is false information disguised as a real report.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence about social media.
practice.answer: I follow someone who posts great science videos.
practice.explanation: Use 'follow someone who...' to describe a creator you subscribe to.

practice.prompt: Lily liked the post and wanted to write a message below it.
practice.text: Lily wrote ___ under the photo of Smarty.
practice.answer: a comment
practice.explanation: A comment is the note you write under a post.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence aloud.
practice.text: Every influencer used the same hashtag this morning.
practice.answer: Every influencer used the same hashtag this morning.
practice.explanation: Great job saying influencer and hashtag clearly.

story.hook: Why did Smarty's morning photo suddenly go viral?

image.describe: Lily and Omar the cats looking excitedly at a laptop screen in the newsroom while Smarty wears tiny glasses.

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: Omar, look at our newsroom profile! Smarty's photo just started to go viral!

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Really? Why did it get so many views?

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: A famous cat influencer shared it with a hashtag for clever cats, and now it is trending!

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Look at the username on this comment—someone says cats cannot read newspapers!

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: Haha, that is fake news! Smarty reads every headline!

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Hundreds of new students want to follow someone from our newsroom, so let us upload another photo and forward the link to Smarty!

questions.prompt: Who shared Smarty's photo?
questions.explanation: Lily says: A famous cat influencer shared it with a hashtag.

questions.explanation: Lily jokes: Haha, that is fake news!

questions.prompt: What happened to Smarty's photo online?

turns.smarty: My photo has hundreds of likes! What happens when a post spreads very fast online?
turns.example: It goes viral.

turns.smarty: Should I add a hashtag or fake news to my next post?
turns.example: Add a hashtag.
turns.hint: Recommend adding a hashtag.

turns.smarty: Someone wrote a nice note under my post. What is that called?
turns.example: It is a comment.

exposure.gloss: the name you choose to use on a website or app
to send a photo, video, or file onto the internet
to send a message or link you received to someone else
being talked about by many users online right now

lessons.title: Advertising
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Tom look at bright adverts in the town and on TV.

items.example: There is a big billboard next to the train station.

lessons.title: An interview
lessons.scenario: Mia interviews a local hero in the newsroom and reports what happened.

items.example: He asked me if the live broadcast started at seven.
items.note: Use 'He asked me if' to report a yes/no question—use statement word order and no question mark.

items.example: She wanted to know where I found the old map.
items.note: Use 'She wanted to know' before 'if' or a question word like 'where', 'why', or 'when'.

items.example: I replied that we were ready to start the interview.
items.note: Say 'I replied that' to report your answer to someone's question.

items.example: The astronaut told us one secret off the record, so we did not print it.
items.note: Say 'off the record' when information is shared privately and must not be published.

items.example: The interviewee smiled and answered every question clearly.
items.note: Use 'the interviewee' for the person who is answering questions in an interview.

items.example: The article tells the hero's adventure in his own words.
items.note: Say 'in his own words' when someone tells a story using the exact style and phrases they spoke.

grammar.title: Reported questions
grammar.explanation: To report a question, change it to normal statement word order (subject before verb) and drop the question mark. Use 'if' for yes/no questions (He asked me if I was ready) and keep the question word for wh-questions (She wanted to know when the train arrived).
examples: He asked me if I worked for the newspaper.
She wanted to know why the report was delayed.

practice.prompt: Ben asked you: 'Are you ready?' Report his question.
practice.text: ___ I was ready for the interview.
practice.answer: He asked me if
practice.explanation: Use 'He asked me if' for a yes/no question from a boy or man.

practice.prompt: Which reported question has the right statement word order?

options: She wanted to know where the interviewee lived.
She wanted to know where did the interviewee live?
She wanted to know where lived the interviewee.
practice.explanation: In reported questions, put the subject (the interviewee) before the verb (lived) with no 'did'.

practice.explanation: Listen for 'I replied that' and 'off the record'.

lessons.title: Telling a story
lessons.canDo: Use past perfect in a story
lessons.scenario: Smarty tells a dramatic mystery story in the newsroom.

items.example: Long ago there lived a clever inventor in a quiet mountain village.
items.note: Start a classic tale or history story with 'Long ago there lived...' to set the scene.

items.example: Our boots were dirty because it had been raining all morning.
items.note: Use 'it had been raining' (past perfect continuous) for rain that continued up to a past moment.

items.example: We reached the station at nine, but by then the last train had left.
items.note: Say 'by then' to mean 'at or before that point in the story'.

items.example: He opened the old box, and what he did not know was that a map was inside.
items.note: Use 'what he did not know' to build mystery when a character misses an important secret.

items.example: Leo found a key that someone had dropped a few days earlier.
items.note: Use 'a few days earlier' with the past perfect to jump back to an earlier event.

items.example: As soon as he had read the letter, he ran to the newsroom.
items.note: Use 'as soon as he had' + past participle to show one action finished right before the next.

grammar.title: Past perfect in narration
grammar.explanation: When telling a story in the past, use the past perfect (had + past participle) for an action that happened before another past action. Use had been + -ing (it had been raining) for a background action that continued up to that moment.
examples: By then, everyone had gone home.
The street was cold because it had been raining.

practice.prompt: Start this traditional tale.
practice.text: ___ a wise painter in a stone tower.
practice.answer: Long ago there lived
practice.explanation: 'Long ago there lived' is a classic story opening.

practice.prompt: Explain why the grass in the park was wet in the story.
practice.text: The park was empty because ___ for hours.
practice.answer: it had been raining
practice.explanation: Use 'it had been raining' for rain continuing before that past moment.

practice.prompt: Match each storytelling phrase with its role in a story.

pairs.right: before that moment in the story

keeping a secret from the hero

lessons.title: Opinions in the media
lessons.scenario: Leo and Zara debate whether news reports are fair and trustworthy.

items.example: In my opinion, every newspaper should check two sources.
items.note: Use 'In my opinion' as a clear, polite way to introduce what you think.

items.text: As far as I am concerned
items.example: As far as I am concerned, a documentary series teaches more than a quiz show.
items.note: Say 'As far as I am concerned' to state your personal view firmly in a discussion.

items.example: I am convinced that fake news is a serious problem online.
items.note: Use 'I am convinced' when you feel completely sure that something is true.

items.example: It seems to me that that headline is trying to scare readers.
items.note: Say 'It seems to me' to give an opinion in a softer, thoughtful way.

items.example: That report is biased because it only shares one side of the story.
items.note: Call a report or writer 'biased' when they unfairly favour one side over another.

items.example: A university science team is a reliable source for climate news.
items.note: A 'reliable source' is a trustworthy place or expert you can depend on for true facts.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its meaning in a media discussion.

pairs.right: I am very sure
from what I can see

a source that is good

practice.explanation: I am convinced = completely sure, It seems to me = soft opinion, biased = one-sided, reliable source = trustworthy.

panels.speaker: Mia
panels.text: Look at our phone! Our latest news article went viral with a catchy hashtag!

panels.speaker: Ben
panels.text: Wait a second. Someone just left a mysterious comment under the front page photo.

image.describe: Ben and Mia the cats looking closely at a glowing laptop screen in the quiet evening newsroom.

panels.speaker: Zara
panels.text: He said that he had found a second key inside the old fortress tower a few days earlier!

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: What he did not know was that we were watching the live broadcast on channel two right then.

panels.speaker: Leo
panels.text: Look at the screen! The presenter is holding an ancient envelope with Smarty's name on it!

image.describe: A television screen in the newsroom showing a cat presenter holding up an old sealed envelope.

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: By then, it had been raining outside for hours, and the midnight train was about to leave.

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: Where did that envelope come from, and who sent it to the studio? Grab your coats—our next adventure starts now!

image.describe: Smarty the black cat putting on his detective scarf by the newsroom door as rain falls outside the window.
